I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'Being looked at sexually' is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision as the index trauma, especially when no other selected items suggest sexual trauma, harassment, or body-focused threat. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for signs that someone is entering the home implies an interpersonal intrusion/assault threat, which does not fit well with a motor vehicle collision and is not supported by the other items. The rest of the threat profile is general hypervigilance to sudden sounds, making this specific home-intruder monitoring item clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes usually implies clothing cues tied to the trauma context. For a motor vehicle collision, this is difficult to justify unless other items indicate clothing-specific trauma reminders, which they do not. It also does not connect plausibly to the selected triggers, which are taste, workplace, and sexual objectification.

Workplace as a trigger is weakly grounded for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision given the rest of the profile: the other trigger and threat items are sensory/accident-related, but nothing in appraisals, threat, or strategies explains why the workplace itself would be a salient trauma cue. This makes the trigger set less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste linked to a motor vehicle collision is possible but clinically unusual, and here it is unsupported by memory content or appraisals that would make a gustatory cue understandable. With no memory items and otherwise sound/crash/vehicle-focused content, this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, a specific taste trigger and an alcohol smell trigger are not impossible, but in combination they imply trauma details (e.g. ingestion, blood, alcohol involvement, hospital/chemical context) that are unsupported by the rest of the profile. The rest of the triggers, threat items, and appraisals are centered on vehicle crash/sound danger, so these sensory triggers look clinically disconnected from the trauma representation described elsewhere.

Undereating as a coping strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and avoidance-based coping around crash-related distress; avoid-driving and screen escape fit that pattern, but food restriction addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, memory, or appraisals. In this profile it appears clinically mismatched rather than a coherent extension of the same trauma-linked cycle.

vignette: Mohammed, a 30-year-old Middle Eastern man divorced from his wife of ten years and working as a tax inspector in Los Angeles, has been grappling with the aftermath of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The accident occurred on a rainy night last year when he was driving home late after working overtime. A car, swerving due to slippery roads and possibly under the influence of alcohol, had collided head-on into his own vehicle. Mohammed vividly remembers the screeching tires, the sudden impact, and the smell of burning rubber and alcohol lingering in the air. Since then, certain triggers have become overwhelmingly potent for him. The crash imagery, the scent of alcohol, and even similar cars on the road can instantly plunge him back into that harrowing moment. Each time he encounters one of these triggers, his body reacts with a surge of adrenaline. For instance, when walking past a bar where patrons are exiting and carrying bottles of beer, Mohammed’s heart races as if the accident is happening again. These experiences have led to severe anxiety and hypervigilance; every unexpected sound or ordinary noise can startle him sharply. To cope with these intense reactions, Mohammed has adopted several maladaptive strategies. He spends long hours on his phone, playing games or browsing the internet, trying to avoid thinking about the accident at all costs. This constant digital escape not only occupies much of his free time but also leaves him feeling disconnected from reality and unable to engage in meaningful activities or relationships. The trauma has profoundly shaken Mohammed’s sense of self-worth and capability. He firmly believes that he can no longer rely on himself, doubting his ability to perform tasks that once defined him as a competent tax inspector. This loss of confidence extends into his personal life; he fears he will never be able to feel normal emotions again. These negative appraisals exacerbate his maladaptive behaviors—his undereating and reliance on digital distractions grow more pronounced, reflecting his deeper distrust in himself. His job as a tax inspector often requires driving to different locations for meetings with clients or other officials. However, the fear of encountering another vehicle accident makes Mohammed avoid driving altogether. This avoidance has practical consequences; he frequently cancels work-related travel plans and arranges teleconferences instead, which leads to increased stress from trying to coordinate remote arrangements and can create tension with his colleagues who depend on face-to-face interactions. Mohammed’s hypervigilance and startle response have also infiltrated his daily life. He is constantly on guard in public spaces like the office or restaurants, where unexpected noises trigger intense fear responses. This heightened state of alertness further reinforces his belief that he cannot trust himself to handle such situations, creating a vicious cycle. The more Mohammed engages in these maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals, the worse his symptoms become. He notices an increasing disconnect between him and his colleagues at work and friends from his past life. His undereating has led to significant weight loss and fatigue, which further diminishes his confidence and ability to function effectively. What finally brought Mohammed to seek help was a realization that he could no longer sustain this level of distress without intervention. The thought of never feeling normal again terrifies him the most, yet he also hopes for a return to a life where he can trust himself and engage fully with the world around him once more.
